idiom_name: Spring Security's SecurityContextHolder on JVM threads; a CoroutineContext element when suspend functions carry the request
implementation_notes: On the JVM the holder is Spring Security's SecurityContextHolder - the same ThreadLocal-backed store used from Java - and a guard reads SecurityContextHolder.getContext().authentication directly. In coroutine code that is not enough, because a coroutine can resume on a different dispatcher thread after a suspension point: the identity has to travel as a CoroutineContext element (the kotlinx.coroutines mechanism whose elements are inherited by child coroutines and can be replaced with withContext), which is exactly what Spring Security's kotlinx-coroutines integration builds when it re-establishes the holder around suspensions. The classic context class is replaced by this holder-plus-element pairing; a hand-written SecurityContextElement is still justified when a suspend guard has no access to the request object, and it must be immutable because child coroutines share it.
pitfalls: A ThreadLocal holder is not coroutine-safe: after a suspension the coroutine may run on another thread, so the holder must be re-established per dispatch or replaced by a CoroutineContext element.
CoroutineContext elements are inherited by child coroutines and must be immutable; rebinding means creating a child scope with withContext, never mutating a shared context object.
Blocking JVM calls inside suspend functions pin work to the wrong thread and defeat dispatcher-based propagation, especially when combined with thread-affine holders.
